prompt: How do you use CMake to build a C++ project?
completion:
## Using CMake to Build a C++ Project  
Below is a practical, step‑by‑step guide that takes you from a fresh source tree to a compiled binary (or library) using **CMake**.  
Feel free to copy‑paste the snippets into your own project and tweak them to fit your needs.

---

## 1. Project Layout (recommended)

```
myproject/                # Root of the source tree
├── CMakeLists.txt        # Root CMake file
├── README.md
├── LICENSE
├── src/                  # Source files
│   ├── main.cpp
│   └── foo.cpp
├── include/              # Header files (optional)
│   └── foo.hpp
└── tests/                # Unit tests (optional)
    └── test_foo.cpp
```

> **Tip** – Keep source (`src/`) and headers (`include/`) separate; this is the layout most people are familiar with.

---

## 2. Minimal `CMakeLists.txt` (Root)

```cmake
# 1️⃣ Minimum CMake version you need
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)

# 2️⃣ Project name & meta‑data
project(MyProject
    VERSION 1.0
    LANGUAGES CXX
)

# 3️⃣ C++ standard (C++17 here, but you can pick any)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)   # Prefer ISO C++ (no GNU extensions)

# 4️⃣ Optional: treat warnings as errors
if (MSVC)
    add_compile_options(/W4 /WX)   # Windows/MSVC
else()
    add_compile_options(-Wall -Wextra -Werror)
endif()

# 5️⃣ Add the executable
add_executable(MyApp
    src/main.cpp
    src/foo.cpp
)

# 6️⃣ Include directories (so `#include <foo.hpp>` works)
target_include_directories(MyApp PRIVATE ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)

# 7️⃣ Link external libraries (optional, e.g. OpenCV)
# find_package(OpenCV REQUIRED)
# target_link_libraries(MyApp PRIVATE OpenCV::OpenCV)

# 8️⃣ Optional: install targets
install(TARGETS MyApp
        RUNTIME DESTINATION bin
        LIBRARY DESTINATION lib
        ARCHIVE DESTINATION lib
)
```

### What each part does

| Line | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `cmake_minimum_required` | Locks in a CMake version that supports the features you’ll use. |
| `project()` | Declares the project name, version, and languages. |
| `set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD ...)` | Enforces a particular C++ standard. |
| `add_compile_options(...)` | Enables strict warning settings. |
| `add_executable()` | Declares a build target (`MyApp`) from listed source files. |
| `target_include_directories()` | Tells the compiler where to find header files. |
| `find_package()` / `target_link_libraries()` | Optional: pulls in third‑party libs. |
| `install()` | Sets up an install rule for `cmake --install`. |

---

## 3. Out‑of‑Source Build (Recommended)

CMake recommends building *outside* the source tree so the source stays clean.

```bash
# From the root of the repo
mkdir build && cd build
cmake ..                      # Configure
cmake --build .               # Compile (default to `Release` if not specified)
```

You can control the build type with an option:

```bash
cmake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug ..   # For debugging
cmake --build . --config Debug      # On MSVC/Visual Studio
```

> **Why out‑of‑source?**  
> * Keeps generated files (e.g., `CMakeCache.txt`, `CMakeFiles/`) out of your source directory.  
> * Makes it easy to delete the whole build tree (`rm -rf build/`) without touching source.

---

## 4. Choosing a Build System Generator

CMake can generate various build system files:

| Generator | Typical Command | Where to use |
|-----------|-----------------|--------------|
| Unix Makefiles | `cmake ..` | Linux/macOS (default on many systems) |
| Ninja | `cmake -G Ninja ..` | When you want fast incremental builds (must install Ninja) |
| Xcode | `cmake -G Xcode ..` | macOS, to open in Xcode |
| Visual Studio | `cmake -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" ..` | Windows |

Example: using Ninja (recommended for speed)

```bash
mkdir build && cd build
cmake -G Ninja ..   # Configure
ninja               # Build
ninja test          # Run tests if you have CTest targets
```

---

## 5. Adding Sub‑Directories

If your project grows, split it into modules:

```
myproject/
├── CMakeLists.txt
├── app/
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt
│   └── ...
├── lib/
│   ├── CMakeLists.txt
│   └── ...
```

Root `CMakeLists.txt`:

```cmake
add_subdirectory(app)
add_subdirectory(lib)
```

In `lib/CMakeLists.txt`:

```cmake
add_library(MyLib
    src/libfoo.cpp
)
target_include_directories(MyLib PUBLIC ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)
```

In `app/CMakeLists.txt`:

```cmake
add_executable(App
    src/main.cpp
)
target_link_libraries(App PRIVATE MyLib)
```

---

## 6. Testing with CTest

Add a simple test:

```cmake
# Root CMakeLists.txt
enable_testing()

add_executable(test_foo tests/test_foo.cpp)
target_link_libraries(test_foo PRIVATE MyLib)
add_test(NAME FooTest COMMAND test_foo)
```

Run tests:

```bash
cmake --build . --target test    # or `ctest` after build
```

---

## 7. Packaging with CPack (Optional)

```cmake
include(CPack)
set(CPACK_PACKAGE_NAME "MyProject")
set(CPACK_PACKAGE_VERSION "${PROJECT_VERSION}")
```

Build a package:

```bash
cpack -G ZIP    # or NSIS, RPM, etc.
```

---

## 8. Common Pitfalls & Quick Fixes

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| `CMake Error: The current CMake version (3.10) is lower than required (3.20)` | You’re using an old CMake | Upgrade CMake (`brew install cmake` on macOS, `apt install cmake` on Ubuntu). |
| `Cannot find OpenCVConfig.cmake` | OpenCV isn’t installed or CMake can’t find it | Install OpenCV or set `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` to its root. |
| Header not found in `#include <foo.hpp>` | Include path missing | Add `target_include_directories()` or `include_directories()`. |
| Linker error: undefined reference to `main` | Wrong target name or wrong file | Ensure `main.cpp` is in the executable source list. |
| Build fails on Windows with `fatal error C1189` | Using a Linux CMake script without porting | Verify path separators (`/` vs `\`), use `WIN32`-specific options. |

---

## 9. Full Working Example (Copy‑Paste)

**`CMakeLists.txt`**

```cmake
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)

project(Sample
    VERSION 0.1
    LANGUAGES CXX
)

set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF)

add_compile_options(-Wall -Wextra -Werror)

add_executable(Sample
    src/main.cpp
    src/hello.cpp
)

target_include_directories(Sample PRIVATE ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)
```

**`src/main.cpp`**

```cpp
#include <iostream>
#include "hello.hpp"

int main() {
    std::cout << hello() << std::endl;
    return 0;
}
```

**`src/hello.cpp`**

```cpp
#include "hello.hpp"

std::string hello() {
    return "Hello, CMake!";
}
```

**`include/hello.hpp`**

```cpp
#pragma once
#include <string>

std::string hello();
```

Build:

```bash
mkdir build && cd build
cmake ..
cmake --build .
./Sample   # prints "Hello, CMake!"
```

---

## 10. Take‑Away Checklist

- [ ] Use **out‑of‑source** builds (`mkdir build && cd build`).
- [ ] Set the C++ standard early (`set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 17)`).
- [ ] Keep your source layout clean (`src/`, `include/`, `tests/`).
- [ ] Add `target_include_directories()` and `target_link_libraries()` **per‑target** (never global).
- [ ] Choose a generator that fits your workflow (Makefiles, Ninja, VS, Xcode).
- [ ] Optionally enable testing (`enable_testing()`) and packaging (`include(CPack)`).
- [ ] Keep your `CMakeLists.txt` minimal and modular – split into sub‑directories when the project grows.

With this foundation you can now build, test, and ship any C++ project using CMake. Happy coding!
